goal: Go from zero ML knowledge to training and evaluating a small image classifier in PyTorch
interpretation: The learner can explain core ML and backpropagation intuition, then write and run a PyTorch training loop for a small CNN image classifier and evaluate it for overfitting and accuracy.
assumptions: The 1200 minutes is pure viewing time, so it covers about 20 hours of videos with no time reserved for practice.
Because the learner likes code-along videos, the plan favors tutorials where the presenter writes code live.
'Small image classifier' means a CNN trained on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST or CIFAR-10, not a large pretrained model pipeline.
Each video or course part should fit within a 90-minute sitting, so long courses are picked in chunks of 90 minutes or less.
Calculus and linear algebra are already known, so math-focused videos should build intuition for ML and not reteach prerequisites.

sub_topics.title: Machine learning fundamentals: models, loss, features, train/test split
sub_topics.why: The learner has no ML background, so they need the vocabulary and framing (supervised learning, loss functions, generalization) before touching neural networks.

sub_topics.title: Gradient descent and backpropagation intuition and math
sub_topics.why: The learner knows calculus, so they can learn the chain rule applied to computation graphs and see how weights are updated, which gives the math intuition they want.

sub_topics.title: PyTorch tensors and autograd
sub_topics.why: The learner knows numpy, so tensors map to familiar ideas. They need to learn the PyTorch API, GPU/device handling, and how autograd computes gradients.

sub_topics.title: Building neural networks and training loops in PyTorch
sub_topics.why: They need to write nn.Module models, pick loss functions and optimizers, use DataLoaders and run the train/eval loop end to end.

sub_topics.title: Convolutional neural networks: convolutions, pooling, architectures
sub_topics.why: Image classification needs CNNs. A linear algebra background helps with understanding convolution as a sliding dot product and with feature maps and shapes.

sub_topics.title: Model evaluation, overfitting, and regularization
sub_topics.why: The learner must measure accuracy and tell whether the model generalizes, using validation splits, loss curves, confusion matrices, data augmentation, dropout and weight decay.

sub_topics.title: Build and train an image classifier end to end in PyTorch
sub_topics.why: A code-along project ties everything together: load an image dataset, build a CNN, train it, evaluate it, and iterate to improve results.

picks.title: [ML1] Machine Learning Fundamentals: Supervised Learning & Linear Regression
picks.reason: Starts from zero with supervised learning: model representation, loss functions and optimization, taught with the math. That suits a learner with a strong math background and no ML. It is flagged pure_theory, but that is what this learner asked for.
picks.confidence_note: Based on the summary only; the card has no verified quotes. Confidence would rise with transcript evidence of depth.

picks.title: Machine Learning Fundamentals: Bias and Variance
picks.reason: Explains bias and variance intuitively. This is the conceptual basis for underfitting, overfitting and train/test behavior, so it sets up the later evaluation material.
picks.confidence_note: Short, well-matched concept video; the flags (pure_theory, surface_intro) are acceptable because the learner wants intuition.

picks.title: Stanford CS229: Machine Learning - Linear Regression and Gradient Descent |  Lecture 2 (Autumn 2018)
picks.reason: A full university lecture on supervised learning, linear regression and gradient descent with the derivations. It uses the calculus and linear algebra the learner already has to give a rigorous ML foundation. At 78 minutes it fits one 90-minute sitting.
picks.confidence_note: Lecture format rather than code-along; the card gives only a summary and the 'likely includes derivations' judgement is unverified.

picks.title: Gradient descent, how neural networks learn | Deep Learning Chapter 2
picks.reason: Gives the visual and mathematical intuition for cost functions, gradient descent and how neural networks learn their weights. This is the math-intuition backbone the learner wants before touching PyTorch.
picks.confidence_note: Clear content match for the sub-topic; there are no verified quotes.

picks.title: Machine Learning Tutorial Python - 4: Gradient Descent and Cost Function
picks.reason: A code-along that implements gradient descent for linear regression in plain Python, covering cost function, MSE and learning rate. It turns the math intuition into numpy-style code the learner can follow.
picks.confidence_note: The segment map lists only the first 15 minutes of a 28-minute video, so the second half is unverified.

picks.title: Backpropagation, intuitively | Deep Learning Chapter 3
picks.reason: Builds intuition for backpropagation, showing how each weight's influence on the cost drives its update. It is the most relevant video in the pool for the backprop concept itself.
picks.confidence_note: Strongest backprop-intuition match; no quotes to verify.

picks.title: Backpropagation calculus | Deep Learning Chapter 4
picks.reason: Gives the chain-rule calculus behind backpropagation, which this learner can follow given their calculus background. It shows how gradients flow backward and prepares them for what autograd automates.
picks.confidence_note: pure_theory flag is desirable here since the learner wants the math.

picks.title: Backpropagation Explained By Hand: Two-Layer Neural Network, Chain Rule and Gradient Descent
picks.reason: Works through a two-layer network by hand with numerical values and checks the analytic gradients against finite differences. A numerical worked example like this fits an engineer, and it previews what autograd will compute.
picks.confidence_note: Content is specific and matches the need; it is a single short video with no quotes.

picks.title: The StatQuest Introduction to PyTorch
picks.reason: A step-by-step PyTorch walkthrough that builds a small network, makes predictions and optimizes parameters with backpropagation. It is the best available coverage of tensors and autograd, though it is flagged surface_intro, and no unflagged candidate covers this sub-topic.
picks.confidence_note: Thin coverage of tensor operations; a dedicated PyTorch tensors/autograd video would be better but none is in the pool. Transcript is poor.

picks.title: Create a Basic Neural Network Model - Deep Learning with PyTorch 5
picks.reason: Code-along showing how to define a PyTorch nn.Module with layers and a forward function. This is the model-building half of the training loop for the learner's first network.
picks.confidence_note: Covers model definition only, not the training step; the training loop is covered later by the CNN code-alongs.

picks.confidence_note: Explains the concept in TensorFlow context, not PyTorch; the concept transfers.

picks.title: Convolutional Neural Networks from Scratch | In Depth

picks.confidence_note: Poor transcript and pure_theory flag; the level is intermediate but suits a math-comfortable learner.

picks.title: Pytorch CNN example (Convolutional Neural Network)

warnings: Under-filled: only about 324 of 1200 minutes are used (~27%), roughly 876 unused. The pool has no long courses and few substantial PyTorch tutorials, and I did not pad with weak or redundant videos.
None of the cards has verified quotes, so evidence_quote_ids is empty for every pick. Reasons rest on the card summaries and metadata, and confidence is moderated for that.

Thin coverage of PyTorch tensors and autograd: the only usable pick is the StatQuest intro, which is flagged surface_intro. Consider supplementing with the official PyTorch tutorials or a longer PyTorch course.
Evaluation coverage is mostly conceptual (bias/variance, regularization). No video clearly shows a train/validation/test split or tracking accuracy in code, so do this yourself in the project.
Sittings: all picks fit within 90 minutes. The 78-minute CS229 lecture should be its own sitting; group the shorter videos into sessions of at most 90 minutes.

Several picks (codebasics CNN explainer, TensorFlow-based) use different tooling for concepts; transfer to PyTorch is assumed. Upload dates of 2026 on a few cards look odd but there is no date floor, so I ignored them.
Practice time is not included in the budget; consider coding along with the videos and reproducing the CIFAR-10 project yourself.
